tagline: Two green volcanic islands, one nation
overview:
Saint Kitts and Nevis is the smallest country in the Americas by both land area and population, a pair of lush volcanic islands in the eastern Caribbean. Saint Kitts, the larger, is shaped like a paddle; Nevis, its round neighbor, lies about three kilometers away across a channel called The Narrows. Together they cover about 261 km², smaller than most cities.

Roughly 48,000 people live here, speaking English. Basseterre on Saint Kitts is the capital, a harbor town with a circular plaza modeled on London's Piccadilly Circus.

The country is a constitutional monarchy with an elected parliament, and Nevis has its own assembly and considerable self-government. For 350 years the islands ran on sugar, until the last cane harvest in 2005; today tourism, offshore finance and a scenic railway built for sugar trains carry the economy. Both islands are green, steep and ringed by beaches of pale and black sand.
landAndNature: Each island is the top of a volcano. Mount Liamuiga on Saint Kitts rises to 1,156 meters and holds a crater lake in its rainforested summit; Nevis Peak, at about 985 meters, wears a permanent cap of cloud, which is how it got its name, from the Spanish for snows. Rainforest, elfin woodland and old sugar terraces cover the slopes, and the coasts alternate between golden sand in the south and dark volcanic sand in the north. Vervet monkeys, brought from Africa in the 1600s, now outnumber people and raid gardens. Hawksbill and leatherback turtles nest on the beaches, hummingbirds feed in gardens year-round, and the surrounding reefs shelter parrotfish, rays and the occasional migrating humpback whale.
peopleAndCulture: Most Kittitians and Nevisians are descended from West Africans brought to the islands in slavery, and their culture blends African, British and Caribbean strands. Carnival, called Sugar Mas, runs from Christmas into early January with calypso competitions, steel pan, big drum music and masquerade troupes in tall feathered headdresses. Goat water, a rich stew of goat meat, breadfruit and dumplings spiced with cloves, is the national dish, served with johnnycakes. Cricket is the great sport, and the islands' players have represented the West Indies team for decades. Alexander Hamilton, a founding father of the United States, was born on Nevis in the 1750s, and his birthplace is now a museum.
history: The Kalinago people, and the Taíno before them, lived here when Christopher Columbus sailed past in 1493. English settlers arrived on Saint Kitts in 1624 and French settlers soon after, and the island became the first successful English colony in the Caribbean, earning it the nickname Mother Colony of the West Indies. Britain and France fought over it repeatedly until Britain gained full control in 1783. Plantation owners enslaved tens of thousands of Africans to cut sugar cane; slavery was abolished throughout the British Caribbean in 1834. The islands were governed with Anguilla until Anguilla broke away in 1967. Saint Kitts and Nevis became fully independent on September 19, 1983, the newest sovereign state in the Americas. Nevis narrowly voted against separating in a 1998 referendum.
funFacts: Saint Kitts and Nevis is the smallest country in the Western Hemisphere in both area and population.
Green vervet monkeys, brought from Africa centuries ago, are thought to outnumber the islands' human residents.
A narrow-gauge railway built to haul sugar cane now carries sightseers on a slow loop around Saint Kitts.
Brimstone Hill Fortress, a huge stone fort built by enslaved laborers, is nicknamed the Gibraltar of the West Indies.
Alexander Hamilton, whose face is on the US ten-dollar bill, was born on the island of Nevis.
